Safemarch Master Lab

Advanced Zscaler
Implementation Guide

Hands-on Master Lab Template

A reusable, advanced Zscaler implementation lab spanning Client Connector, ZIA, DNS, DLP/EDM, ZPA private applications, Browser Access, Private Service Edge / Universal ZTNA, logging, and OneAPI-based administration. Individual courses, workshops and demos can be distilled from this master lab.

Approx. Core Practice Time14 hr 20 min
Lab ModelReusable master environment / build learner objects
Safemarch Master Lab • 2026 Edition • Rev 21.1
Lab Foundation

Safemarch Master Lab Network Layout

The master environment uses two isolated networks. The Office network hosts the learner endpoint and the new idp VM; the Data Center network hosts private applications and Zscaler infrastructure. The dual-homed Private Service Edge is present on both networks for the Phase 4 Universal ZTNA exercise, but it is not used as an IP router.

VM and Service Inventory

NetworkVM / HostAddressPrimary Purpose in the Master Lab
OfficeWindows Client / ZCC192.168.1.1Learner endpoint for Client Connector, ZIA, ZPA, DNS, Browser Access and policy validation.
Officeidp192.168.1.252Office DNS server and external Keycloak IdP. Keycloak/External IdP configuration is reserved for a later master-lab extension and is not configured in Rev 20.
Office + DCzpa-service-edge192.168.1.10 / 10.0.0.10Dual-homed ZPA Private Service Edge for the Universal ZTNA task. IP forwarding remains disabled.

Index

Lab Structure

The lab uses a continuous Safemarch deployment storyline. Each phase builds objects and policy behavior that later phases reuse. Tasks specify business goals, mandatory values, expected outcomes, concise validation where it adds unique evidence, hints, and documentation.

Phase 1 — Endpoint Foundation & Device TrustDesired-state identity → trusted network → Z-Tunnel 2.0 → Windows App Profile/PAC → process bypass → alternate Service Edge → Z-Tunnel 1.0 vs TWLP → ZIA Device TrustApprox. 200 minPhase 2 — Secure Internet AccessTLS inspection → URL/SaaS controls → QUIC → DNS steering → DoH-to-ZTR translation → iterative DNS transit → DNS Gateway routing → Sandbox → File Type Control → NSS streamingApprox. 295 minPhase 3 — Protect Corporate DataPredefined DLP → custom classification → Exact Data Match (EDM) → approved business exception → reusable cloud-app risk governanceApprox. 115 min + summaryPhase 4 — Publish Private Applications SecurelyOAuth App Connector → app publication → access policy → trusted-network + device posture + session hardening → Browser Access + user portal → ZPA-to-ZIA file inspection → Private Service Edge / Universal ZTNA → ZPA log streamingApprox. 190 minPhase 5 — Automate AdministrationScoped OneAPI client → Postman OAuth → ZPA inventory → automated SOC watchlist updateApprox. 60 min
Approximate total core task time: 13 hours 45 minutes across Phases 1–5. The expanded master guide intentionally exceeds 8 hours so participants can try more scenarios across a broader implementation curriculum; summary/review pages are not timed tasks.
Before You Begin

Lab Conventions

Default-setting ruleAny parameter or option not explicitly specified in a task should retain the appropriate product default. Do not change unrelated settings.
Policy and Resource NavigationConfiguration tables that ask you to create or modify an enforcement rule use Policy Path. Reusable objects that are referenced by policies use Resource Path. These rows identify the Zscaler Admin Console navigation path; ordinary geographic or infrastructure Location fields keep their normal meaning.
Log-correlation conventionFor tasks that require Insights validation, record the test time before generating traffic. On Windows PowerShell, use $t=Get-Date; "Local: $($t.ToString('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff zzz'))"; "UTC: $($t.ToUniversalTime().ToString('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff')) UTC". Use the UTC value as the primary correlation timestamp and search a small window around it in ZIA/ZPA logs.
Pilot-user authenticationUse the lab-provided initial password for Maya Shah and Daniel Lee. If the tenant or identity flow prompts for 2FA/MFA, complete the lab/instructor-provided authentication method. Do not disable MFA or change unrelated authentication policy merely to complete the exercise.
Identity baselineMaya Shah and Daniel Lee are preconfigured pilot users with Internet & SaaS (ZIA) and Private Access (ZPA) service entitlements. Do not recreate the users or change their service entitlements. Phase 1 creates only the Finance and Marketing user groups and their memberships.
  • [N] represents the student number assigned to the training pod.
  • The exercise starts from a clean training baseline with Maya Shah and Daniel Lee already created and entitled to ZIA and ZPA. Learners create the Finance and Marketing groups and the remaining task objects.
  • Tasks are build/configure exercises rather than deliberately pre-broken troubleshooting scenarios.
  • Use only the tenant and virtual machines assigned to your pod.
  • Task instructions describe required outcomes rather than supplying click-by-click answers.
  • Expected Outcome defines success. Validation is intentionally brief and adds only distinct evidence that is worth checking.
Phase 1

Endpoint Foundation & Device Trust

Build a deterministic endpoint foundation without assuming a clean tenant: establish identity and service entitlements, recognize the Safemarch Office network, configure Z-Tunnel 2.0 and the Windows App Profile, prove PAC and process-specific bypass behavior, troubleshoot Service Edge selection, compare Z-Tunnel 1.0 with TWLP, and finish by deriving ZIA Device Trust from Windows posture.

1. Identity & EntitlementsReach the required Maya/Daniel, Finance/Marketing and service-entitlement state using local or external identity sources.
2. Forwarding FoundationRecognize Safemarch-Corporate, use Z-Tunnel 2.0 and verify the Windows packet-filter component.
3. Endpoint PolicyApply the Windows App Profile, protection controls, certificate, Debug logging and an exact-host PAC bypass.
4. Forwarding DiagnosticsDemonstrate process bypass, temporary same-cloud Service Edge selection, and Z-Tunnel 1.0 vs TWLP behavior.
5. Device TrustBuild Internet & SaaS posture and prove a High → Medium → High trust transition for the same endpoint.
Time guide: approximately 200 minutes.

Part C — Enable Z-Tunnel 2.0 web/PAC integration

SettingRequired StateWhy it matters
Redirect Web Traffic to Zscaler Client Connector Listening ProxyEnabledMoves applicable web traffic through the local ZCC listening proxy so the App Profile PAC in Task 3 can make a DIRECT decision for a specific host.
Use Z-Tunnel 2.0 for Proxied Web TrafficEnabledAfter the PAC is evaluated, web traffic that is not bypassed continues over Z-Tunnel 2.0 instead of being sent by Z-Tunnel 1.0.
Why both settings are required for this lab.If the listening-proxy redirect is disabled, do not expect the Task 3 App Profile PAC to govern the normal packet-filter Z-Tunnel 2.0 web path. If redirect is enabled but Use Z-Tunnel 2.0 for Proxied Web Traffic is disabled, the PAC can still be evaluated, but forwarded web traffic from the listening proxy uses Z-Tunnel 1.0.

Part D — Verify the Windows packet-filter component

Run the targeted validation first:

Get-NetAdapterBinding -AllBindings -IncludeHidden -ComponentID ZS_ZAPPRD |
    Format-Table Name, DisplayName, ComponentID, Enabled -AutoSize

For the current Safemarch Windows image, the expected result is Zscaler Lightweight Filter, component ID ZS_ZAPPRD, with Enabled = True on applicable adapters. Adapter names and the number of bindings will vary.

Broader troubleshooting query
Get-NetAdapterBinding -AllBindings -IncludeHidden |
    Where-Object {
        $_.DisplayName -match 'Zscaler' -or
        $_.ComponentID -match 'Zscaler|^ZS_'
    } |
    Format-Table Name, DisplayName, ComponentID, Enabled -AutoSize
Optional: verify the signed Zscaler driver package in the Windows driver store
pnputil /enum-drivers |
    Select-String -Pattern "Zscaler" -Context 3,6

The driver version is informational and will change with the ZCC build. Do not make a specific version number a pass/fail criterion.

Expected OutcomeThe endpoint can distinguish the Safemarch Office network, use the intended Z-Tunnel 2.0 transport behavior, evaluate the Task 3 PAC at the ZCC listening proxy, and has an enabled Zscaler packet-filter component.

1. Establish the forwarded baseline

2. Build and assign the custom PAC

  2. Near the beginning of FindProxyForURL(url, host), before the normal Zscaler forwarding returns, add:
if (host == "ipinfo.io") {

  1. Verify and deploy the PAC.
  2. Copy its HTTPS Hosted URL and assign it as the App Profile Custom PAC URL.
  3. Use Update Policy in ZCC.

Bypass a Specific Windows Process and Interpret the Forwarding Evidence

Part A — Establish and interpret the before state

curl.exe -s https://ip.zscaler.com?json
JSON fieldInterpretation
srcipSource address seen by the verification service. On a Zscaler-proxied path this commonly reflects the Zscaler service/proxy path rather than the endpoint's own public/NAT address.
vipZscaler Service Edge / VIP handling the transaction.
nodenameZscaler processing node.
datacenterZscaler processing data center.
xffClient-side public/NAT source information conveyed through X-Forwarded-For. This is not the endpoint's private 192.168.1.1 address.
clientipClient public IP identified by the service for the transaction.

PlatformWindows

New-navigation detail.The current Application Bypass documentation places the page under Infrastructure → Common Resources → Application → IP Based; that page can create both IP-based and process-based application bypass objects.

RequirementValue

App ProfileSafemarch-Windows-Pilot
Install WFP DriverEnabled

Save, use Update Policy, and close/restart any existing curl.exe process before retesting.

Part D — Prove selective bypass

  1. Run the same curl.exe -s https://ip.zscaler.com?json command again.
  2. Compare the before/after JSON and Web Insights visibility. The direct process should no longer look like a normal Zscaler-processed web transaction.
  3. In Edge/Chrome, open https://ip.zscaler.com and confirm browser traffic still follows Z-Tunnel 2.0.
Expected OutcomeThe bypass is process-specific rather than destination-wide: curl.exe uses the direct path, while the browser remains protected.

Phase 1 — Task 5

Temporarily Override the Z-Tunnel 2.0 Public Service Edge

Phase 1Moderate–HighApprox. 25 min
Business GoalDiscover an alternate ZIA SVPN VIP in the correct tenant cloud, temporarily steer Z-Tunnel 2.0 web traffic to it for troubleshooting, prove the Service Edge change, and restore automatic proximity selection.
Service Edge selection — normal proximity vs temporary troubleshooting override
Normal state
Windows ClientZ-Tunnel 2.0
→
Automatic Service Edge${GATEWAY} / proximity selection
→
InternetWeb Insights: Data Center A
Temporary test state
Windows ClientZ-Tunnel 2.0 request
→
Alternate SVPN VIPLearner-selected from the exact tenant cloud
→
InternetWeb Insights: Data Center B
This task changes the Z-Tunnel 2.0 Service Edge for troubleshooting. It is not a destination-specific country-egress design.

Part A — Record the normal processing location

  1. Use a browser to open https://ip.zscaler.com and record the current cloud / processing location.
  2. Generate a normal web transaction and record the Data Center field in Web Insights.
Do not use curl for this task.Task 4 intentionally bypasses curl.exe; use the browser to avoid contaminating the Service Edge comparison.

Part B — Select your own alternate SVPN VIP

  1. Determine the exact Internet & SaaS cloud assigned to the tenant/account from the Account Settings menu in Experience Center.
  2. Open https://config.zscaler.com/<YOUR-ZSCALER-CLOUD>/cenr.
  3. Select an active SVPN VIP for a different Zscaler data-center location.
  4. For a predictable exercise, preferably choose a different country/location in the same continent or broad region. This is a lab-design recommendation, not a Zscaler requirement.
Exact-cloud requirement.Use only an SVPN VIP listed for the tenant's own Zscaler cloud. Do not select a VIP from another cloud merely because the geography is convenient.

Part C — Apply the temporary PAC override

Edit Safemarch-Pilot.pac. Preserve the ipinfo.io → DIRECT logic above the tunnel-selection logic, then add the selected alternate SVPN VIP:

var tunnel2 = "${ZT2_REQUEST}";
if (tunnel2 == "true") {
    return "PROXY <SELECTED_ALTERNATE_SVPN_VIP>:443; PROXY ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY}:443; DIRECT";
}

Part D — Prove and restore

  1. Deploy the PAC and use Update Policy. Reconnect Internet & SaaS if necessary to establish a new session.
  2. Repeat the browser and Web Insights checks. Confirm the processing Data Center changed.
  3. Remove the temporary alternate-SVPN logic and restore the normal ${GATEWAY} / ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY} proximity-based behavior.
  4. Update policy again and confirm normal selection is restored.
Expected OutcomeThe learner can independently locate a valid same-cloud SVPN VIP, temporarily alter Z-Tunnel 2.0 Service Edge selection, prove the change, and return the endpoint to the standard proximity-based state.

This exercise compares capture behavior. Z-Tunnel 2.0 remains the normal Safemarch forwarding baseline and is restored at the end.

Part A — Repeatable no-proxy test

Add-Type -AssemblyName System.Net.Http
$handler = New-Object System.Net.Http.HttpClientHandler
$handler.UseProxy = $false
$client = New-Object System.Net.Http.HttpClient($handler)
$client.GetStringAsync('https://ip.zscaler.com?json').Result

Part B — Test Tunnel with Z-Tunnel 1.0

RequirementTemporary Value
Resource PathInfrastructure → Connectors → Client → Forwarding Profile for Platforms
Internet & SaaS ActionTunnel
DriverPacket Filter-Based
Tunnel VersionZ-Tunnel 1.0

Refresh policy, test the browser and the PowerShell request, then inspect the Windows runtime state:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Zscaler\App' |
    Select-Object ZNW_State, ZWS_State, ZPA_State

On the Safemarch Windows build, expect ZWS_State = TUNNEL_FORWARDING. The PowerShell request that explicitly ignores the Windows proxy should still be captured and show Zscaler egress.

Part C — Test Tunnel with Local Proxy

Change the same forwarding profile to Tunnel with Local Proxy, save, and refresh policy. Run the same registry command again. On the Safemarch Windows build, expect ZWS_State = LOCAL_PROXY_FORWARDING.

Also inspect the Windows system-proxy state:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings' |
    Select-Object ProxyEnable, ProxyServer, AutoConfigURL

Do not require one fixed PAC URL; the important observation is that TWLP enforces the Windows proxy/PAC path. Repeat the browser test and the UseProxy = $false PowerShell request. The browser should remain protected, while the no-proxy request should go direct.

Optional log proof.If the registry state is unavailable or you want deeper troubleshooting evidence, search ZSATunnel logs for getSmeProxyState. Zscaler's current troubleshooting runbook documents states including TUNNEL_FORWARDING and LOCAL_PROXY_FORWARDING.

Part D — Operational decision guide

ConditionPreferReason
Modern normal Windows deploymentZ-Tunnel 2.0Preferred baseline; broader port/protocol coverage than Z-Tunnel 1.0.
Need transparent capture of web traffic, including applications that ignore the system proxyZ-Tunnel 1.0 / TunnelNetwork/packet-filter interception does not depend on application proxy awareness.
Z-Tunnel 2.0 is unsuitable because of network/firewall/UDP behavior, but web traffic still needs a TCP-oriented protected pathZ-Tunnel 1.0Useful as a fallback/hybrid web path.
Packet-filter/tunnel interoperability causes issues with a full-tunnel VPN or local applicationTWLPProxy-based application-layer forwarding can avoid the conflicting interception behavior.
Applications can safely be required to honor system proxy/PAC settingsTWLPTWLP is appropriate when proxy-based capture is intentional and its coverage limits are understood.
Do not treat TWLP as equivalent coverage to Tunnel mode.A client that intentionally ignores the system proxy can escape the TWLP web path unless another control captures or blocks it. That is exactly what the no-proxy PowerShell test demonstrates.

Part E — Mandatory restore

Restore Safemarch-Standard-Forwarding to the Phase 1 baseline: Z-Tunnel 2.0, On-Trusted TLS, Off-Trusted DTLS with TLS fallback, Private Access enabled, and both Task 2 proxied-web settings enabled. Refresh policy and confirm normal Z-Tunnel 2.0 operation.

Part E — Prove High → Medium → High

View the enrolled endpoint at Infrastructure → Connectors → Client → Device Overview, open Device Details, and locate Device Trust Level.

  1. With corp-device.txt present and Windows Firewall active, verify High.
  2. Rename the marker:

  1. Wait for posture reevaluation and establish a fresh connection if necessary. Verify Medium.
  2. Restore the marker:
Rename-Item C:\Users\student\corp-device.disabled corp-device.txt
  1. After reevaluation, verify High again.
Posture changes are not necessarily instantaneous.Allow the configured evaluation interval and use a new connection when validating the updated state. Existing connections are not automatically reclassified solely because the posture value changed.

Part F — Policy use is deferred to Phase 2

The High / Medium / Low Device Trust Level created here is available as a condition in applicable Internet & SaaS policies. Phase 2 should consume this signal in an actual ZIA policy so the learner can prove that the same user and same destination receive a different outcome solely because the device trust level changed.

Cleanup automation limitation.The Safemarch cleanup automation does not currently have a fully validated create/delete lifecycle for every Device Posture and Internet & SaaS Posture Profile object used here. An automated tenant reset can therefore leave posture resources behind. During manual reset, first remove dependent App Profile/policy references, then review Policies → Common Configuration → Resources → Internet & SaaS Posture Profiles and ... → Device Posture for stale Safemarch objects.
Expected OutcomeThe endpoint visibly transitions High → Medium → High using deterministic Windows posture, and Safemarch-ZIA-Trust is ready to be consumed by Phase 2 Internet & SaaS policy.

Phase 1 completion

Phase 1 Desired State

  • Identity and service entitlements are deterministic but not tied to a single identity source.
  • The Office network is recognized as Safemarch-Corporate.
  • Normal Windows Internet traffic uses the Z-Tunnel 2.0 baseline and the packet-filter component is validated.
  • The Windows App Profile uses protection controls, certificate deployment, Debug logging, and a proven exact-host PAC bypass.
  • Selective process bypass and alternate-Service-Edge troubleshooting have been demonstrated and restored.
  • The learner can distinguish Z-Tunnel 1.0 network capture from TWLP local-proxy capture on Windows.
  • ZIA Device Trust is established and validated, ready for policy consumption in Phase 2.
Phase 2

Secure Internet Access

Build Safemarch's Internet security policy stack in a logical sequence: establish TLS visibility, create justified decryption exceptions, control risky destinations, govern SaaS activity and tenant access, preserve inspection through network controls, then explore DNS steering, DoH-to-ZTR protocol translation, iterative DNS transit, selective DNS Gateway routing, Sandbox analysis, File Type Control and real-time NSS log streaming.

1. VisibilityTLS baseline plus privacy and certificate-pinning exceptions.
2. Destination & SaaS ControlURL policy, SOC watchlist, GenAI and Microsoft 365 tenant governance.
3. Network & DNSQUIC control, DNS observation/steering, DoH-to-ZTR protocol translation, iterative DNS transit and selective DNS Gateway routing.
4. Threat & OperationsSandbox higher-risk downloads, file-type enforcement/evasion testing, and NSS streaming of blocked web activity.
Time guide: approximately 295 minutes.

Phase 2 — Task 12

Diagnose and Support Iterative DNS with DNS Transit

Phase 2Tough / HighApprox. 30 min
Business GoalSafemarch operates DNS infrastructure that can perform iterative resolution. Emulate an iterative resolver from the Windows Client, prove why the predefined Zscaler Trusted DNS Resolver path breaks non-recursive queries, then build a selective DNS Transit rule and use Firewall + DNS Insights to explain the before/after behavior.
Recursive vs iterative DNS — simple distinctionWith recursive DNS, a client asks one recursive resolver for the final answer and that resolver performs the upstream work on the client's behalf. With iterative DNS, the resolver follows referrals itself: Root → TLD → authoritative server. Each response can point to a different next DNS server, so the destination IP changes as resolution progresses. The manual -norecurse queries in this task emulate those iterative hops.
Recursive DNS vs iterative DNS
Recursive — one resolver returns the final answer
Client“Resolve www.example.com for me”
→
Recursive ResolverHandles Root, TLD and authoritative lookups internally
→
Final AnswerClient receives the resolved result
Iterative — the resolver follows referrals
Resolver → Rootcom. NS
→
Resolver → .com TLDexample.com. NS
→
Resolver → AuthoritativeFollows the final delegation
Key point for this lab: ZTR is intended to act as a recursive resolver. An iterative resolver must be able to keep changing its destination as it follows referrals, which is why DNS Transit is needed.
Why the default ZTR path fails — and what DNS Transit changes
Default behavior
RD=0 QueryTarget = root/TLD server
→
ZTR NAT RuleRedirects dest:53 to ZTR
→
FailureZTR does not resolve iterative queries
DNS Transit
RD=0 QueryTarget = root/TLD server
→
Higher-Rank NAT RuleDNAT IP/FQDN blank
Port 53
→
Original DNS ServerDestination is preserved and the referral succeeds
Lab simplificationThe Windows Client is emulating an iterative resolver by sending manual non-recursive queries with nslookup -norecurse. A production design would normally scope the transit rule to the source IP of the real iterative DNS server, not to an end-user account.

Part A — Prepare a Log-Friendly Baseline

  1. Temporarily edit Safemarch-Windows-Pilot and clear the DNS Domain Inclusion value *. Keep the private-domain exclusion unchanged. Save the App Profile, then on the Client PC use Update Policy in ZCC and allow Client Connector to refresh.
  2. This temporary change is only to keep the public DNS server selected in the command visible as Client Destination IP in Firewall Insights. The public UDP/53 flow still enters ZIA through Z-Tunnel 2.0 in this lab.
  3. Record the UTC timestamp and run the first non-recursive query:
$t=Get-Date
"Local: $($t.ToString('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff zzz'))"
"UTC:   $($t.ToUniversalTime().ToString('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff')) UTC"
nslookup -norecurse -type=NS com. 198.41.0.4

Without a higher-ranked transit rule, expect the query to fail (for example, Server failed).

Find the baseline evidence
Firewall Insights filterClient Destination IP = 198.41.0.4
Firewall columnsEvent Time, Client Destination IP, Client Destination Port, DNAT Rule Name, Server Destination IP, Traffic Forwarding, Bypassed Session, Flow Type
DNS Insights filtersRequested Domain = com and, where useful, DNS Request Type = NS
DNS columnsDNS Error Code, Server IP, Resolver Gateway, Request Rule Name, Event Time
Correlate with the UTC timestamp using a small time window. The key clue is that the client targeted A-root, but ZIA matched the predefined Zscaler Trusted DNS Resolver path and the actual server-side destination no longer remains A-root.

RequirementMandatory Value
Policy PathPolicies → Access Control → Firewall → NAT Control
Rule NameSafemarch-Iterative-DNS-Transit

Network ServiceDNS
Destination198.41.0.4 — intentionally narrow for the first test
ActionDNAT IP/FQDN & Port
DNAT IP/FQDNLeave blank
DNAT Port53

What port-only DNAT means hereBy specifying destination port 53 but no replacement IP/FQDN, the original DNS destination in the request is preserved. This is the DNS Transit behavior used for iterative queries.

Part C — Prove the Root Hop Works

  1. Activate the rule.
  2. Repeat nslookup -norecurse -type=NS com. 198.41.0.4.
  3. Confirm that the command now returns the .com delegation / gTLD name servers.
  4. In Firewall Insights, filter Client Destination IP = 198.41.0.4. Confirm the custom rule matched and the Server Destination IP remains 198.41.0.4.
Do not over-trust one DNS error-code fieldReferral-style responses can be represented differently in DNS tools/logs. For this step, the strongest evidence is the usable .com referral in nslookup plus Firewall Insights showing the original root-server destination preserved by Safemarch-Iterative-DNS-Transit.

Part D — Follow the Referral and Discover the Incomplete Design

Use one of the returned .com TLD servers. The lab uses 192.5.6.30 (a.gtld-servers.net):

$t=Get-Date
"UTC: $($t.ToUniversalTime().ToString('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff')) UTC"
nslookup -norecurse -type=NS example.com. 192.5.6.30

The query is expected to fail while the NAT rule is restricted to 198.41.0.4.

Find the second-hop failureIn Firewall Insights, filter Client Destination IP = 192.5.6.30. The query no longer matches the narrow Safemarch rule, so it falls through to Zscaler Trusted DNS Resolver. In DNS Insights, filter Requested Domain = example.com and review DNS Request Type, DNS Error Code, Server IP and Resolver Gateway.

Part E — Correct the Transit Design

  1. Edit Safemarch-Iterative-DNS-Transit and remove the destination-IP restriction. Keep the practice-user/source scope, Network Service = DNS, and the port-only DNAT action.
  2. Activate the change.
  3. Repeat both tests:
nslookup -norecurse -type=NS com. 198.41.0.4
nslookup -norecurse -type=NS example.com. 192.5.6.30

Both non-recursive hops should now reach the DNS servers explicitly selected in the commands. Use Firewall Insights to show that each Client Destination IP is also retained as the corresponding Server Destination IP under the Safemarch transit rule.

Production design lessonAn iterative resolver changes destination as it follows referrals. Therefore, production policy normally identifies the source IP of the iterative DNS resolver and transits its DNS traffic, rather than creating destination-specific exceptions for individual root/TLD/authoritative servers. A broad rule scoped only to an end user would also transit that user's ordinary recursive DNS, which is why this user-based scope is temporary and lab-only.
Root-server fallbackUse A-root 198.41.0.4 as the normal lab target. If the instructor confirms that A-root is unreachable from the training pod for reasons unrelated to ZIA policy, use B-root 170.247.170.2 as the fallback. Replace the root-server IP consistently in the initial narrow rule and the root-query command; do not switch roots merely because the expected pre-transit query fails.

Part F — Restore the Normal Lab Baseline

Cleanup / restore checkpoint Complete the steps in this section before moving on. These temporary lab changes can affect later tasks if they are left in place.
  1. Disable or delete Safemarch-Iterative-DNS-Transit.
  2. Restore DNS Domain Inclusion = * in Safemarch-Windows-Pilot, save the App Profile, then use Update Policy in ZCC on the Client PC.
  3. Confirm ordinary Internet DNS returns to the ZTR/DNS Control design established in P2-T10. This restored state is required for the next DNS Gateway task.
Expected OutcomeThe learner explains why ZTR disrupts iterative DNS, proves that a port-53-only higher-ranked NAT rule preserves the intended DNS destination, discovers why destination-specific transit is incomplete, and corrects the policy so multiple iterative hops can transit ZIA.
Unique validation: Show three correlated states: (1) A-root query redirected to ZTR and fails, (2) A-root succeeds under the narrow transit rule while the .com TLD hop still falls through to ZTR, and (3) after removing the destination restriction, both root and TLD queries preserve their requested server destinations and succeed.

AI Instant Verdict — interpreting threat scoresHigher scores indicate greater suspicion. A score of 40 is not “good”; it is the low end of the configurable suspicious threshold range. For Sandbox Suspicious with Quarantine, the configurable Minimum Threat Score is 40–70; files below the configured threshold can be allowed. Scores 70–90 can trigger additional quarantine behavior with Allow and Scan, while scores above 90 are treated as high-confidence malicious and blocked. Exact behavior still follows the selected Sandbox rule actions.

Part B — Rename the File Extension and Retest

  1. Make a copy of P2_T15_PDF_EXPECT_BLOCK.pdf and rename only the filename extension to P2_T15_PDF_RENAMED.txt. Do not convert or edit the file contents.

  4. In Web Insights, compare Upload File Name with Upload File Type. The filename now ends in .txt, but the service identifies the underlying PDF file type.
Key conceptRenaming a file is not the same as converting it. File Type Control can use true file-type detection rather than trusting only the filename extension.

Part C — Place the Renamed File Inside a ZIP Archive

Create a normal, non-password-protected ZIP containing the renamed file. On Windows PowerShell, one simple method is:

Compress-Archive -Path .\P2_T15_PDF_RENAMED.txt -DestinationPath .\P2_T15_PDF_IN_ZIP.zip -Force
  1. Do not add ZIP/Archive as a blocked file type in Safemarch-Finance-PDF-Upload-Block; the purpose is to test the PDF inside the archive.
  2. Upload P2_T15_PDF_IN_ZIP.zip to the same destination.
  3. Confirm the transfer is blocked because the recognized PDF is detected inside the supported archive.
  4. Use Web Insights to compare Upload File Name, Upload File Type, and Unscannable Type with the earlier tests.
Expected OutcomeA normal ZIP archive does not provide a simple bypass for the PDF-only rule: the service can inspect supported archive contents and enforce File Type Control on the recognized file inside.
Optional exploration — Password-Protected ArchiveCreate a password-protected ZIP containing the same PDF test file and upload it. Before testing, review Policies → Cybersecurity → Inline Security → Malware Protection → Security Exceptions → Password-Protected Files. When Password-Protected Files = Block, the protected archive is blocked by Malware Protection because its contents cannot be scanned; this is a different enforcement reason from the normal ZIP/File Type Control test. In Web Insights, review Unscannable Type, Upload File Name, and Upload File Type to identify the behavior; the unscannable classification for a password-protected/encrypted file can appear as Encrypted File. Do not change the Malware Protection setting merely to force File Type Control to inspect an encrypted archive.
Unique validation:Compare the normal TXT, original PDF, PDF renamed to .txt, and normal ZIP containing the renamed PDF. Explain why the first is allowed while the other three are blocked. If the optional password-protected ZIP is tested, identify that Malware Protection—not normal archive inspection—is responsible for the block when Password-Protected Files is set to Block.

Stop/continue rule: when an enforcing policy blocks the transaction, the request stops at that point. If the matched action permits or continues evaluation, the transaction proceeds to the next applicable control. Not every request traverses every policy family.

Why order mattersIf File Type Control blocks an uploaded PDF first, DLP does not get a second opportunity to inspect that blocked transaction. This is why policy precedence can change which control appears as the enforcement reason in logs.

Phase 3

Protect Corporate Data

Safemarch has established secure Internet access and SaaS controls. The next step is to protect regulated financial information, Safemarch-specific confidential content, and exact employee records without blocking legitimate business workflows. This phase introduces Exact Data Match (EDM) with the Zscaler Index Tool, then extends the same governance mindset to cloud applications. The DLP exercises use native ZIA capabilities and synthetic lab data only.

1. Regulated DataUse a predefined DLP engine to block payment-related data leakage.
2. Company DataCreate a custom patterns-and-phrases dictionary and DLP engine.
3. Exact Data MatchConfigure the Index Tool, index synthetic employee records, and enforce same-record EDM correlation.
4. Business ExceptionPermit classified data only through an approved Microsoft 365 workflow.
5. Cloud-App Risk GovernanceApprove ChatGPT explicitly, define one reusable high-risk profile, and apply it across AI/ML and File Sharing policies.
6. ReviewConnect content protection, exact-record matching, and application-risk governance.
Time guide: approximately 115 minutes, plus a short summary review

Phase 3 — Task 3

Protect Exact Employee Records with Exact Data Match (EDM)

Phase 3HighApprox. 45 min
Business GoalSafemarch wants to prevent disclosure of known employee records without relying on broad patterns that can produce false positives. Build an Exact Data Match (EDM) workflow using the Zscaler Index Tool, index synthetic employee records, require the employee ID plus both name fields from the same indexed record, and block only validated full-record matches.
EDM workflow — from structured source data to DLP enforcement
Synthetic CSV8 employee records
Index Toolindex-vm
10.0.0.8
EDM TemplateEmployee_ID + First_Name + Last_Name
EDM DictionaryPrimary + all secondary fields
DLP EngineWeb channel
DLP PolicyFinance upload → Block
Key idea: EDM does not merely look for three unrelated strings. It validates values against indexed structured records and can require the primary and secondary fields to correlate to the same record.
⚠ Pre-task cleanup — EDM templates are not removed by the lab cleanup automationBefore creating the new template, open Policies → Data Protection → Common Resources → Data Classification → Index Templates → Exact Data Match and remove stale Safemarch lab EDM templates from previous sessions. Do not delete unrelated/shared templates. The cleanup automation does not currently remove EDM templates imported into Experience Center, so stale objects can remain after an otherwise successful cleanup.

Part A — Download the Synthetic EDM Test Kit

Part C — Create the Index Tool Configuration and Install Its Client Certificate

  1. In Experience Center / ZIA, go to Policies → Data Protection → Common Resources → Data Classification → Index Tool.
  2. Add an Index Tool configuration with VM Name = index-vm and Status = Enabled. Save and activate the change.
  3. From the Index Tool configuration, download the SSL client certificate package. Save the ZIP as index-vm.zip for the lab.
  4. Copy index-vm.zip to the zsroot home directory on 10.0.0.8. Use the lab file-transfer method. If OpenSSH/SCP is available on the Windows client, an example is:
    scp "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\index-vm.zip" zsroot@10.0.0.8:/home/zsroot/index-vm.zip
  5. On index-vm, install the downloaded client certificate using the lab-validated ZADP command:
    cd /home/zsroot sudo zadp configure AdpClientCertificate index-vm.zip
  6. Enter the password supplied for the certificate package when prompted. The Index Tool service stops/reconfigures as needed and checks cloud connectivity.
Useful ZADP commandsUse these when validating or recovering the Index Tool VM. The service normally updates automatically after initial configuration; use the manual update sequence only when needed.
CommandPurpose
sudo zadp statusConfirm whether the Index Tool service is running.
sudo zadp troubleshootRun certificate, cloud-connectivity, service and update checks.
sudo zadp stopStop the service before a manual update.
sudo zadp update-nowInstall an available Index Tool update after the service is stopped.
sudo zadp startStart the service after update/configuration.
sudo zadp restartRestart the Index Tool service.
sudo zadp status sudo zadp troubleshoot # Only if a manual update is required: sudo zadp stop sudo zadp update-now sudo zadp start sudo zadp status

Phase 3 Review

Corporate Data Protection and SaaS Risk Summary

Phase 3 combines five complementary control patterns: reuse Zscaler's predefined knowledge for regulated data, define Safemarch-specific classification, use Exact Data Match to correlate known structured records, create a narrow exception for a legitimate corporate workflow, and reuse a centralized cloud-application risk definition across multiple SaaS categories.

Data / WorkflowControl ImplementedExpected Result
Synthetic PCI-sensitive content from FinancePredefined PCI engine + Safemarch-Finance-PCI-BlockBlocked to Internet/cloud destinations.
Safemarch confidential phrase + project identifierCustom dictionary + Safemarch-Confidential-EngineRecognized as Safemarch-specific confidential content.
Synthetic employee record containing Employee_ID + First_Name + Last_Name from the same indexed rowSafemarch-EDM-Employee-Dictionary + Safemarch-EDM-Employee-EngineBlocked for Finance; incomplete or cross-record combinations remain allowed.
Safemarch confidential project file to ordinary Internet/cloud destinationSafemarch-Confidential-Upload-BlockBlocked.
Safemarch confidential project file to approved Microsoft OneDrive workflowSafemarch-Confidential-M365-AllowAllowed for Finance.
PCI-sensitive content to approved Microsoft OneDrive workflowPCI policy remains in forceBlocked.
Approved ChatGPTTemporary Sanctioned / Risk 2 governance demonstration plus the explicit P2-T07 ChatGPT ruleExcluded from the high-risk profile during the test but still subject to explicit granular controls.
Unsanctioned high-risk AI applicationSafemarch-Unapproved-Risky-Apps + Safemarch-Risky-AIApplication access blocked.
Unsanctioned high-risk File Sharing applicationSame risk profile + Safemarch-Risky-FileSharingViewing allowed; uploading blocked.
Phase 3 Expected OutcomeSafemarch can protect both broad data classes and exact known records: regulated and company-specific information receive DLP enforcement, EDM correlates synthetic employee fields to the same indexed record, legitimate Microsoft 365 workflow can be narrowly exempted, and a reusable application-risk definition can drive different Cloud App Control outcomes across AI/ML and File Sharing.
Phase 4

Publish Private Applications Securely

Safemarch is ready to move its internal web, Windows administration, and Linux administration services behind Zscaler Private Access. Deploy the App Connector infrastructure, publish the applications, apply least-privilege access, then harden privileged administration with trusted-network context, device posture and stricter session controls. Build three lightweight temporary web services for Browser Access and a user portal, prove that a Client Connector private-app download can be inspected by ZIA File Type Control, then extend the same ZTNA policy model to on-premises users with a locally deployed Private Service Edge before operationalizing the deployment with ZPA Log Streaming.

1. ConnectivityEnroll the supplied App Connector VM using OAuth 2.0.
2. ApplicationsPublish Web, RDP and SSH application segments through the connector.
3. Least PrivilegeMap application access to the Safemarch pilot identities.
4. Harden & PublishAdd Trusted Network + device posture + timeout controls, then publish browser-only applications through a user portal.
5. Inspect, Localize & OperateRoute a ZPA private-app download through ZIA File Type Control, localize trusted-network brokerage with a Private Service Edge, then configure ZPA log streaming.
Time guide: approximately 190 minutes.

Part C — Add a Privileged Timeout Policy

RequirementMandatory Value
Policy PathPolicies → Access Control → Private Applications → Timeout Policy
Rule NameSafemarch-Privileged-Timeout
Authentication TimeoutSpecific Interval — 8 hours
Idle Connection TimeoutSpecific Interval — 15 minutes
Application Segment GroupSafemarch-Admin-Apps
Rule OrderPlace the custom privileged rule above the Default Timeout Policy rule.
Other CriteriaDo not duplicate the access-policy identity/posture criteria unless specifically required; the timeout rule is scoped by the privileged application group.
Authentication Timeout vs Idle Connection Timeout Authentication Timeout is the maximum age of the user's current ZPA authentication before access to a matching application requires fresh authentication. It is evaluated when the user attempts to access an application. Idle Connection Timeout controls how long an application connection may remain inactive before ZPA ends that connection. An idle timeout expiration does not by itself force ZPA reauthentication.
Important reauthentication nuanceA successful ZPA reauthentication obtains a new SAML assertion and refreshes the user's authentication timestamp across ZPA. Therefore the 8-hour privileged rule does not maintain an isolated authentication clock. Instead, it requires the user's most recent ZPA authentication to be no more than 8 hours old when a privileged application is accessed. A successful reauthentication for a privileged app also refreshes the timer used by applications with longer timeout requirements.
Two meanings of “Default”The Default Timeout Policy rule is the catch-all baseline and currently requires authentication every 7 days while not ending sessions because of an idle timeout. Separately, the Default option inside an Idle Connection Timeout field uses protocol connection defaults (for example, an open TCP connection has a 2-hour default idle timeout). This lab avoids that ambiguity by explicitly setting the privileged idle interval to 15 minutes.

  1. On the Windows Client PC, run Test-Path 'C:\Users\student\corp-device.txt' and confirm the local PowerShell result is True. This confirms the marker file exists; do not expect the Zscaler Admin Portal to display a live True/False value for this file check.
  2. Confirm Safemarch-General-Access still contains no Trusted Network or posture requirement.
  3. Confirm Safemarch-Admin-Access is configured for Maya + Safemarch-Admin-Apps + Safemarch-Corporate + Safemarch-Corp-Device-Posture = VERIFIED.
  4. Allow enough time for Client Connector posture evaluation/refresh, then validate the privileged application access behavior where practical.
  5. Confirm Safemarch-Privileged-Timeout is scoped to Safemarch-Admin-Apps with the required 8-hour authentication timeout and 15-minute idle timeout.
  6. If practical, establish an SSH or RDP session and leave it idle long enough to observe the custom idle behavior. Waiting eight hours to test the authentication timeout is not required.

Unique validation: Explain why the general and admin access contexts differ, and explain why a successful privileged-app reauthentication also refreshes the authentication timestamp used by applications with longer timeout settings.

Phase 4 — Task 5

Build and Publish Web Applications with Browser Access and a User Portal

Phase 4Moderate - ToughApprox. 35 min
Business GoalBuild three lightweight Safemarch web applications on the supplied lab server, publish them with Browser Access, expose them through a single user portal, and compare the user-facing external URL with the private internal URL reached by the App Connector.
You will build the web resourcesUse the Corp: SIEM Server at 10.0.0.2 to create three simple temporary HTTP services: Intranet on TCP 8080, Finance on TCP 8081, and Admin on TCP 8082. Use the assigned {unique-student-ID} in the private FQDNs shown in Part B; all three names resolve to this server. These are short-lived lab resources; persistent systemd services are not required.

Part A — Build the Three Temporary Web Servers

Open a terminal on Corp: SIEM Server. Create three directories and a simple page for each application:

mkdir -p ~/safemarch-ba-web/{intranet,finance,admin}

printf '%s\n' '<!doctype html><html><body style="font-family:Arial;background:#eaf2ff;padding:40px"><h1>Safemarch Intranet</h1><p>Safemarch Browser Access lab - TCP 8080</p></body></html>' > ~/safemarch-ba-web/intranet/index.html

printf '%s\n' '<!doctype html><html><body style="font-family:Arial;background:#eaf8ef;padding:40px"><h1>Safemarch Finance</h1><p>Safemarch Browser Access lab - TCP 8081</p></body></html>' > ~/safemarch-ba-web/finance/index.html

printf '%s\n' '<!doctype html><html><body style="font-family:Arial;background:#fff0df;padding:40px"><h1>Safemarch Admin</h1><p>Safemarch Browser Access lab - TCP 8082</p></body></html>' > ~/safemarch-ba-web/admin/index.html

Start one temporary Python HTTP server for each directory:

nohup python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 0.0.0.0 --directory ~/safemarch-ba-web/intranet >/tmp/safemarch-ba-intranet.log 2>&1 &
nohup python3 -m http.server 8081 --bind 0.0.0.0 --directory ~/safemarch-ba-web/finance >/tmp/safemarch-ba-finance.log 2>&1 &
nohup python3 -m http.server 8082 --bind 0.0.0.0 --directory ~/safemarch-ba-web/admin >/tmp/safemarch-ba-admin.log 2>&1 &

Confirm all three services answer locally:

curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8080
curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8081
curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8082
Expected local resultEach command returns an HTTP success response and the three temporary web resources are ready for ZPA publication. No persistent service configuration is required for this exercise.

Phase 4 — Task 7

Implement Universal ZTNA with a ZPA Private Service Edge

Phase 4Moderate–HighApprox. 35 min
Business Goal Safemarch already publishes the intranet through ZPA and enforces the access policies built earlier in Phase 4. Extend that existing ZTNA design to on-premises users by enrolling a locally hosted ZPA Private Service Edge (PSE), prioritizing it for the Safemarch-Corporate trusted network, and proving that the same private application is brokered locally without giving the Office network ordinary routed access to the Data Center network.
Important baseline difference from a fresh ZPA deployment Tasks 1–6 have already created the App Connector, application segments and access policies. Therefore, http://intranet.safemarch.com should normally work before this task through the existing ZPA Service Edge path. This task does not use “application unavailable before PSE” as evidence. Instead, capture the current Service Edge, deploy the PSE, then prove that the same application and policy use the Private Service Edge while direct backend access remains unavailable.

  1. On the Windows Client PC, confirm Client Connector shows Private Access = Connected.

Part B — Create the Private Service Edge Group and Provisioning Key

  1. Go to Infrastructure → Private Access → Component → Private Service Edges and click Add.
  2. Create a new provisioning key and associate it with a new Private Service Edge group using the following mandatory values.
RequirementMandatory Value

Part C — Verify the Dual-NIC PSE Network and Enroll the Appliance

Open the console of the supplied ZPA Private Service Edge VM. The two NICs are preconfigured by the lab builder; learners verify them but do not redesign Skytap routing.

ip -br addr
ip route
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
CheckExpected Result
Office-side interface192.168.1.10/24
Data Center-side interface10.0.0.10/24
Default routeOne normal default route through the Office-side network (lab baseline)
Direct DC route10.0.0.0/24 through the Data Center NIC
Linux IP forwardingnet.ipv4.ip_forward = 0
Do not enable routingThe PSE is dual-homed so ZCC and the App Connector can each reach a local interface. Do not enable Linux IP forwarding and do not enable general Skytap inter-network routing. The PSE must broker ZPA sessions rather than become a conventional router between the Office and Data Center networks.

Apply the provisioning key to the preinstalled appliance:

sudo systemctl stop zpa-service-edge
sudo touch /opt/zscaler/var/service-edge/provision_key
sudo chmod 644 /opt/zscaler/var/service-edge/provision_key
echo "<PSE_PROVISIONING_KEY>" | sudo tee /opt/zscaler/var/service-edge/provision_key
sudo test -s /opt/zscaler/var/service-edge/provision_key && echo "Provisioning key file present"
sudo systemctl start zpa-service-edge
sudo systemctl status zpa-service-edge --no-pager
Secret handlingDo not paste the provisioning key into screenshots, shared notes or the participant answer sheet. The command above writes it to the expected appliance file; the validation deliberately checks that the file is non-empty instead of printing the key back to the terminal.

Verify that the running PSE is listening for ZPA connections:

sudo ss -lntp | grep ':443'

Confirm the Private Service Edge also appears as connected/healthy in the ZPA Admin Console.

Part D — Prove App Connector-to-PSE TCP/443 Reachability

On the ZPA App Connector at 10.0.0.3, verify that the new PSE interface on the Data Center network is reachable:

ping -c 3 10.0.0.10
curl -vk --connect-timeout 5 https://10.0.0.10
How to interpret the curl test The important evidence is Connected to 10.0.0.10 ... port 443. The PSE TCP/443 listener is a ZPA service endpoint, not a generic HTTPS web server. A subsequent TLS reset such as curl: (35) ... Connection reset by peer can therefore occur and does not invalidate the TCP reachability test. By contrast, Connection refused means no process is listening, while a timeout suggests a network/firewall path problem.

Part E — Use the PSE FOHH Table to Prove Both Local ZPA Connections

On the Private Service Edge, run the following diagnostic:

curl localhost:8500/fohh/servers?small

Do not focus on the long dynamic IDs. Identify the local/remote IP addresses and the connection state.

Evidence in OutputInterpretation
[192.168.1.10]:443 ... [192.168.1.1]:<ephemeral-port>Windows Client Connector has a direct ZPA connection to the Office-side PSE interface.
[10.0.0.10]:443 ... [10.0.0.3]:<ephemeral-port>App Connector has a direct ZPA connection to the Data Center-side PSE interface.
fohh_connection_connectedThe listed FOHH relationship is connected.
If only one side appearsFirst confirm that the missing component is still configured and healthy in the tenant. A cleaned or deleted App Connector object can prevent the expected PSE relationship even when basic IP/TCP reachability is correct. Do not immediately enable inter-network routing as a workaround.

    Test-NetConnection 10.0.0.2 -Port 80
  2. Confirm direct IP connectivity remains unavailable while http://intranet.safemarch.com continues to work for the authorized user through ZPA.
  3. Explain the result: the PSE moved the ZPA broker location into the local environment; it did not create routed network access from the Office subnet to the Data Center subnet.
Expected Outcome The Office endpoint still cannot directly reach the private backend network, but the authorized user accesses the existing intranet through ZPA. The PSE FOHH table shows direct Client Connector and App Connector relationships to the dual-homed Private Service Edge, and ZPA User Activity identifies Safemarch-PSE-Group as the Service Edge path for the application transaction.

customerIdLab-provided ZPA Customer ID
Use the variables already defined by the imported OneAPI collection The current Zscaler OneAPI Postman collection already defines standard collection variables such as oneAPIBaseUrl, ZIABaseUrl, and ZPABaseUrl. Do not duplicate these variables in the lab environment. In the imported collection, ZIABaseUrl is derived from {{oneAPIBaseUrl}}/zia/api/v1 and ZPABaseUrl is derived from {{oneAPIBaseUrl}}/zpa.

Phase 5 — Task 3

Retrieve the ZPA Deployment Inventory

Phase 5EasyApprox. 10 min
Business Goal Use the read-only ZPA scope to confirm that automation can discover the private-application deployment created in Phase 4.

Request 1 — Application Segments

Method: GET
Request URL:
{{ZPABaseUrl}}/mgmtconfig/v1/admin/customers/{{customerId}}/application

Locate the following application segments in the response and record their IDs and configured domain/FQDN values:

  • Safemarch-Intranet
  • Safemarch-RDP
  • Safemarch-SSH
Practical API tip — search by a known nameWhen you already know the application segment name, the list endpoint can be searched directly instead of returning the full inventory first:
Method: GET
Request URL:
{{ZPABaseUrl}}/mgmtconfig/v1/admin/customers/{{customerId}}/application?search=Safemarch-Intranet
Verify the returned name if more than one result is returned. The ID-based endpoint remains the deterministic way to retrieve one known object once its ID is available.

Request 2 — App Connector Groups

Method: GET
Request URL:
{{ZPABaseUrl}}/mgmtconfig/v1/admin/customers/{{customerId}}/appConnectorGroup

Confirm that Safemarch-Corp-Connectors appears in the response and record its ID.

Expected Outcome Both GET requests return HTTP 200 and the learner can identify the ZPA objects created in Phase 4 without any write permission.

Phase 5 — Task 4

Automate the Safemarch SOC Watchlist

Phase 5Easy–ModerateApprox. 15 min
Business Goal The SOC receives new indicators frequently. Use OneAPI to add two harmless training indicators to the Safemarch-SOC-Watchlist created in Phase 2, without replacing its existing entries.

Step 1 — Find the Custom Category ID

Method: GET
Request URL:
{{ZIABaseUrl}}/urlCategories?customOnly=true

OneAPI reference: Get URL Categories

Find Safemarch-SOC-Watchlist. Record its id, configuredName and superCategory values.

Step 2 — Incrementally Add Indicators

Method: PUT
Request URL:
{{ZIABaseUrl}}/urlCategories/{{categoryId}}?action=ADD_TO_LIST

OneAPI reference: Update URL Category

Set {{categoryId}} to the ID returned in Step 1. Use the current configuredName and superCategory values returned by the GET request.

{ "configuredName": "<configuredName returned by Step 1>", "superCategory": "<superCategory returned by Step 1>", "dbCategorizedUrls": [ "alpha.example.com", "beta.example.com" ] }
Why these fields? For a custom URL-category PUT, include both configuredName and superCategory from the current category object. Phase 2 intentionally created the SOC watchlist using URLs that retain their parent category, so add the new indicators to dbCategorizedUrls. The ADD_TO_LIST action appends the new entries without replacing the existing list.

Step 3 — Activate the ZIA Change

Method: POST
Request URL:
{{ZIABaseUrl}}/status/activate

Step 4 — Verify

Method: GET
Request URL:
{{ZIABaseUrl}}/urlCategories/{{categoryId}}

Confirm that the two new indicators appear under the parent-category-retaining URL field and that the original Phase 2 entries remain present.

Expected Outcome Safemarch-SOC-Watchlist retains its existing entries and now also contains alpha.example.com and beta.example.com. The configuration change is activated through OneAPI.
